1#main: The laws of orlah—where it applies and for whom. In it are 28 seifim. One who plants a food tree counts three years from the time of its planting, and all fruit that will be on it within three years are forbidden in benefit forever—whether the essence of the fruit, the pits, or the shells, such as walnut shells and pomegranate rinds, and their sap and dyes, and grape pits and the beer made from them, and unripe fruit (pagim), and dates that do not cook—and grapes that were scalded and do not finish in their cooking—all are liable for orlah and exempt from revai. And there are those who forbid dates that do not cook even for revai.
2#main: But the leaves, lulavim, and vine water—that is, when one cuts the vine and it drips like water—are permitted regarding orlah.
3#main: Poor man's cakes (ebionot), palm hearts (temarot), and caper berries of the caper bush are liable for orlah. In what case is this said? In Eretz Yisrael; but in the Diaspora, ebionot are liable and temarot and caper berries are exempt.
4#main: These three years are not counted day by day; rather one follows the years of the world, which begin from Tishrei. And if it was a leap year, it is a leap year for orlah and for revai. And sometimes there are only two years and a day, and sometimes more than three years. How so? If he planted before the sixteenth of Av and there still remained forty-four days until Rosh Chodesh Tishrei—once Rosh Chodesh Tishrei arrives, a year is counted for it and it counts two more years. And if he planted on the sixteenth, from the sixteenth onward he counts three complete years from the coming Rosh Chodesh Tishrei; and after Rosh Chodesh Tishrei of the fourth year, all fruit that chanata in it before the fifteenth of Shevat have the status of orlah as well, even though they complete later. And what chanata from the fifteenth of Shevat of the fourth year until the fifteenth of Shevat of the fifth year are called revai; and after the fifteenth of Shevat of the fifth year they are fully permitted.
5#main: That which we said that after Rosh Chodesh Tishrei of the fourth year, all fruit that chanata before the fifteenth of Shevat have the status of orlah even though they complete later—this is specifically in a planting where we were lenient at its beginning, since because forty-four days passed for it a year was counted; therefore we were stringent at its end. If not so, no. And some say there is no difference.
6#main: Revai fruits have the status of maaser sheni for every matter. And in the time of the Beit HaMikdash they had to bring them up to Jerusalem to eat them there, or redeem them and bring the redemption money there. And they are permitted immediately after redemption. And nowadays, when one cannot bring them to Jerusalem, one redeems them after they are complete and detached. And one may redeem all of them for the value of a perutah even if they are many; and one throws the perutah into the Great Sea, or pulverizes it and scatters it to the wind, or throws it into a river after pulverizing it. And one recites a blessing at the time of redemption: "Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of revai." Or one redeems with fruits that are worth a perutah, which is one thirty-second of a ma'ah of silver—that is, an aspero Ottomanis, which weighs sixteen barley grains, which is a quarter of a drachma (his own wording). {Rama: And the regular coin in these lands—the half and the vinar—is more than the value of a perutah, and one redeems on it (Terumat HaDeshen siman 192).} Revai fruits are exempt from leket, shichecha, pe'ah, and olelot.
7#main: The law of netah revai applies even in the Diaspora. And there are those who say it applies only in Eretz Yisrael, but in the Diaspora fruits that come after the two years of orlah are permitted without redemption. {Rama: And some say it does not apply in the Diaspora except in a vineyard and not in other trees (Tur in the name of the Geonim, Ramban, and Rosh, and so it appears).}
8#main: Orlah applies in every place and at every time, both in that of a non-Jew and in that of an Israelite; except that in Eretz Yisrael it is d'oraisa and in the Diaspora it is halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai. {Rama: And it is forbidden to gather orlah fruits for a non-Jew, because one benefits from the good will the non-Jew feels toward him on account of this (Kol Bo and Beit Yosef in the name of Orach Chaim).}
9#main: A doubt of orlah in Eretz Yisrael is forbidden; in the Diaspora it is permitted. How so? A vineyard that has plantings of orlah and grapes are sold outside it—in Eretz Yisrael it is forbidden; in Syria it is permitted when he did not know they were brought from that vineyard. And in the Diaspora it is permitted even if he knows they were brought from that vineyard, provided it does not appear they were harvested from orlah plantings. {Rama: And all the more so a vineyard that is a doubt of orlah is permitted (so it appears from the Tur, Rosh, and Mordechai on the first chapter of Kiddushin).}
10#main: A vineyard that is a doubt of orlah—in Eretz Yisrael it is forbidden; in Syria it is permitted; and needless to say in the Diaspora.
11#main: A barrel of wine hidden in an orlah vineyard is permitted, for a thief does not steal from this vineyard and hide it within. But grapes found hidden in it are forbidden, for it is likely he stole them from it and hid them within.
12#main: It is forbidden to plant orlah fruit; and if he planted, the fruit that comes from it is permitted—both this and that cause permitted. And it is permitted to plant a branch (yachor—that is, a branch from the tree) of orlah, for orlah applies only to fruit.
13#main: A non-Jew and an Israelite who were partners in a planting—if they did not stipulate at the beginning, it is forbidden. And if they stipulated at the beginning of the partnership that the non-Jew would eat the two years of orlah and the Israelite would eat the three permitted years corresponding to the two years of orlah—this is permitted, provided they do not come to an accounting, such as calculating how much fruit the non-Jew ate in the two years of orlah until the Israelite eats corresponding to those fruits—for this is forbidden because it is like exchanging orlah fruits. {Rama: And there are those who permit even if they did not stipulate at the beginning, only that the Israelite says to the non-Jew: take you the two years of orlah and I will take two permitted years corresponding to them (Tur and Rosh).}
14#main: It is permitted to say to a non-Jew in the years of orlah: work my vineyard and take its fruits, and give me your vineyard that has passed two years of orlah and I will work it and take its fruits.
15#main: It is permitted to sell a non-Jew fruits of the two years of orlah for the three years that have not yet come.
16#main: Whether one plants a kernel or a branch, or uproots the whole tree and plants it elsewhere, or grafts a branch onto another tree, or layers (buries a branch in the ground—that is, he makes a hollow next to the tree and lowers one of the tree's branches and buries its middle in the hollow and its head emerges from the other side and it becomes a tree)—all are liable for orlah. And this is specifically when he cut it from this side of the trunk of the tree, or that it does not draw nourishment from it; but as long as it is attached and draws nourishment from it, it is considered one of its branches and is exempt. And if after the layered branch grew he layered another branch in the ground and did so many times one after another—as long as the first is attached to the trunk of the tree, all are exempt. If the first was disconnected from the trunk of the tree, they are liable and begin counting for them from when it was disconnected, and the trunk is exempt. And if the trunk was uprooted from the ground, it returns to be subsidiary to the branch that was layered, and one counts for both the trunk and the branch from when it was uprooted.
17#main: Even though it is the custom of farmers to layer vines every year, it is permitted to drink wine from non-Jewish vineyards because a doubt of orlah is permitted. And even in vineyards that Israelites work and layer every year it is permitted, because one who layers and grafts is liable for orlah only in Eretz Yisrael but not in the Diaspora. And one can find permission also for children of Eretz Yisrael in wine of non-Jewish vineyards, because the majority of vines are not orlah. And even in vineyards known with certainty to contain orlah, one may permit them because before two years of orlah pass they do not produce fruit; and if they produce, they are thin and weak and unfit to make wine from.
18#main: A tree that was cut down and grew back from the root is not liable unless it was cut from above the ground, and one counts for it from the time of cutting. But if anything of it remained, it is exempt.
19#main: A tree that wind uprooted or a river swept away and carried to another place, and the soil around its roots went with it and he added soil there and it took root there in the ground—we estimate it: if it could live on the original soil that came with it without additional soil afterward, behold this is like planted in its place and exempt from orlah; and if not, it is liable.
20#main: A tree that was uprooted and roots remained attached, even the thickness of a needle—that with which one stretches a garment after weaving—it is known it can live without additional soil, and it is exempt even if he added much soil.
21#main: A shoot that is not a tefach high is liable for orlah forever because of marit ayin, for it appears as though it is in its first year. In what case is this said? In one planting, or even two corresponding to two with one tail protruding. But if the whole vineyard is so, it is permitted, for it has publicity.
22#main: A layering that was disconnected while full of fruit; and likewise an old tree that was uprooted with fruit on it and replanted elsewhere; or one took a branch full of fruit from an old tree and grafted it onto a young tree—if the fruit increased so that the original permitted fruit is not one part in one hundred of the addition, it is forbidden; if not, it is permitted. But if he grafted a branch full of orlah fruit into an old tree, the fruits of the branch are forbidden forever, even if they grew greatly.
23#main: One who plants a food tree and does not intend it for eating but to be a fence for a field, or for the wood to burn or for building, is exempt—provided it is evident it is not for eating: if for burning, that they are planted close together and he does not space tree from tree as appropriate; if for building, that he prunes the branches so they thicken; if for a fence, that it is in a place that needs fencing. And even if one side, whether inner or outer, whether lower or upper, is for one of these purposes and the other side for eating—the side for eating is liable and the rest exempt. And if he later intended it for eating, it is liable for orlah and revai and one counts from the time of planting. But if he did not intend it until the end of the third year, it has no status of revai, for there is no revai without orlah. And if he planted it for food and afterward intended it for one of these, he is liable.
24#main: One who plants for the sake of a mitzvah, such as for a lulav or etrog, is liable.
25#main: One who plants in his own property for the sake of the public is liable.
26#main: One who plants in the public domain; and a robber who plants; and a non-Jew who plants, whether for himself or for an Israelite; and one who plants in a house; and on a roof that he filled with earth and planted in it; and one who plants in a ship or in a pot—even though it is not perforated, he is liable.
27#main: What grows on its own in private domain is liable; in a place of rocks (trashim—that is, hard, strong stones) it is exempt. And even one who plants in an uninhabited place is exempt, provided he does not do enough tending that he tends its fruits until he brings them to settlement; but if he does enough tending, he is liable.
28#main: A non-Jew who was selling fruits and said they are orlah or netah revai is not believed—even if he said he bought them from so-and-so.
